facts.fact_text: The applicant's husband, Mr Kutlu Adalı, was a Turkish Cypriot writer and journalist.
Mr Kutlu Adalı was known for having written and published articles strongly criticising the policies and practices of the Turkish Government and the authorities of the "TRNC".
For the last seven years before his death, Mr Kutlu Adalı wrote regularly for Yenidüzen, a left-wing newspaper.
On the anniversary of Kutlu Adalı's death the applicant organised a ceremony to commemorate her husband.

The "TRNC" regime refused to register an association called the "Kutlu Adalı Foundation", whose aims include the furthering of the ideas of Kutlu Adalı regarding peace, democracy, human rights and freedom.

On 20 June 1997 the public authorities prevented the applicant and her daughter from attending a meeting organised by a radio station in southern Cyprus, by not giving them permission to cross over to the southern part of Cyprus.
On the anniversary of Kutlu Adalı's death the applicant organised a ceremony to commemorate her husband.
On the day of the commemoration ceremony for Kutlu Adalı, the municipality brought in digging machines to dig up the road just under the applicant's street.
A picture of Kutlu Adalı, which was displayed in the applicant's garden, was stolen.
Before the applicant left for England, a real-estate agent came to meet her daughter and told her to sell their house and accept any offer he would make to buy it.
The applicant contends that following her application to the European Court of Human Rights, her daughter was dismissed from her post in a bank.

On 2 April 1998 the Nicosia Family Court ordered the registration of the Kutlu Adalı Foundation after the applicant and eight other persons followed the correct procedure.
The applicant complained of the inadequacy of the investigation launched by the "TRNC" authorities into the death of Kutlu Adalı.
The applicant complained that following the death of her husband she had been subjected to continuing practices of harassment, intimidation and discrimination by the "TRNC" authorities.
The applicant and her husband received various threats intended to deter Mr Kutlu Adalı from continuing to express his opinions.
Between January 1980 and July 1996, unknown persons subjected Mr Kutlu Adalı to various forms of harassment.
Mr Kutlu Adalı's house was attacked with machine guns.
Mr Kutlu Adalı received frequent threatening phone calls.
Unknown people entered Mr Kutlu Adalı's house looking for copies of his articles, in order to be able to start criminal proceedings against him, as he was writing his articles under a pseudonym.
After the publication of the article about the St Barnabas monastery theft, Mr Kutlu Adalı began to receive frequent threatening phone calls.
The "TRNC" authorities refused to show the applicant her husband's body.
The applicant was told by the doctor in charge of the mortuary, Dr İsmail Bundak, that no post mortem had been carried out, although the body had been X-rayed.
The applicant was never allowed to see the X-rays of her husband's body.
The applicant was informed for the first time that a post mortem had been carried out in the Government's observations of 1 April 1999, and a copy of the post-mortem report was provided at that time.
The police refused to start an investigation based on the anonymous phone call, stating that the woman caller was known for making false allegations to the police.
The applicant gave copies of the article containing the threat from the head of the "Grey Wolves" to the police to investigate, but she did not receive any response.
The applicant did not receive any concrete information in reply to her letter of 26 June 1997 to the security forces' commander, Mr Hasan Peker Günal.
Plain-clothes policemen have constantly been following the applicant and her daughter.
The applicant's and her daughter's phones had been tapped and their correspondence monitored.
The applicant and her daughter received anonymous phone calls.
The applicant's telephone and fax line has been disconnected from time to time.
The applicant maintains that the water supply of her house has been cut on several occasions and she does not believe that this was due to technical faults as alleged by the Council Water Department.

In his concluding remarks, police assistant inspector Ahmet Soyalan stated that it had not been possible to identify the murderer(s) of Mr Kutlu Adalı and that he could not therefore reach a positive result for the investigation.
The coroner stated that the murderer(s) of Kutlu Adalı could not be identified and declared the case closed.

Shortly after Mr Kutlu Adalı had been killed, a large number of police officers went into the applicant's house, ostensibly to guarantee the security of the house because, according to them, they found the door open and the television switched on.
The police officers who entered the applicant's house turned everything upside down and it took the applicant and her family two years to restore order amongst her husband's books and papers.
The applicant was of the opinion that the security forces were opposed to an effective investigation being carried out into the killing of her husband.
The applicant had been subjected to constant harassment after the death of her husband, including receiving threatening telephone calls.
The applicant's complaints to the police, both orally and in writing, about the harassment she experienced led to nothing.
